Wallet side: you move over to your wallet of choice where you have your ada stored: Yoroi, Nami, Gero, Deadalus. This part will be vary slightly due to the wallets having different interfaces, I'll be covering Yoroi in this example. 
1. Click the send tab at the top of the page and Paste the copied address in the "receiver" box. 
2. Type in the EXACT ada amount the NFT website told you to put, in the "amount" box. The wallet will take a moment to calculate the fees that will be needed for the transaction.
3. Once it's done calculating (this may take a bit depending on what's going on with the network) you can hit next. A confirmation box will pop up with a brief description of what your about to do and a place to enter your password. Once you've entered your password and hit confirm, all that's left is to watch your transactions and wait for the NFT to show up in your wallet! AGAIN this is NOT an example of what cornucopias will do, but a general overview on how minting on cardano works. Currently there's no staking. And by staking I mean the one where you add a token and receive the same token over time. Similar to ADA staking.

What's now active is LP token farming. Pancake swap is an Automated Market Maker, for that to work you need liquidity pools for each pair of tokens available for swapping.

A liquidity pool is a basket of the two tokens that are getting swapped. In our case BNB and COPI. (edited)
Friday, December 24, 2021 at 6:37 AM
To provide liquidity to a pool you need 50% of one token and 50% of the other token.
In our case, let's say 100 COPI and WBNB in the equivalent value (aprox 0.0138)
When you add those two to a liquidity pool they are taken out of your wallet and in return you get a Liquidity Provider Token.
Imagine leaving your coat at a garderobe. For it you get a token so you can claim it back
That's exactly what the LP token is for. It exist so you can claim back your COPI and WBNB you left in the liquidity pool.

Ok, a little bit of a description of how DEXs work, why there are liquidity pools and why should we care:
Please explain wise one

DEXs, Decentralised Exchanges, work using one of 2 methods. Either a Order Book system or an Automated Market Maker system.

Imagine the Orderbook one as a market place. Token sellers display their tokens and prices on the market stalls. Token buyers, come in, select the merchant, and select the batch of tokens they want to buy.

The issue here is that sellers need to wait for buyers. And buyers must buy in batches at the price the seller wants.

The other one, the AMM, or Automated Market Maker solves this issue. If you are a buyer: you come in, select how many tokens you want to buy at the market price and done. As a seller: you come in, select how many you want to sell at the market price and done. No waiting.

But to make it work, there must be a liquidity pool. Meaning that when swaps are made, the tokens get added and removed from an existing pile.

Say I want to trade my apples for oranges. In an AMM system, you come to the trading table and on the table there are already 2 piles. One of oranges, the other of apples. To trade, I leave my apples in the apple pile and take the oranges (of the equivalent value as the apples I left in the apple pile) I want from the orange pile.

Those two piles must exist for the system to work. That means, others must bring in apples and oranges to create those 2 piles, before I can swap my apples for oranges. Once the 2 piles have been made, trading in the apple/orange pair can occur.

Since no one is altruistic to just leave their oranges and apples, there's 2 incentive mechanisms to insure the 2 piles are always stocked up. 
One is the "Liquidity Provider Fee". In our example, each time an apple is exchanged for and orange or conversely an orange is exchanged for an apple a fee is added to the transaction.

That liquidity provider fee is then distributed to all the ones that have provided the apples and oranges to the 2 piles. Proportional to the amount of apples and oranges they brought for the 2 piles. (edited)
Friday, December 24, 2021 at 10:57 AM

Also to ensure that people don't bring only oranges, or only apples and thus make one pile too small or non-existent, you are forced by the system to bring 50% apples and 50% oranges.

Let's say that 1 orange is 2 apples. If you want to bring 100 oranges to the pile you also need to provide 200 apples to the apple pile.

Once you deposited your 100 oranges and 200 apples you get a token. That token represents those 300 fruits you left in the piles. At a later date you can use your token to retrieve the 300 fruits from that pile.
This brings us to the second incentive used to keep the 2 fruit piles always stocked up. It's called "Token Farming".

In our example, the orange and apple cultivators have decided to make a small fund of let's say a million oranges. And they say: "Each day we will distribute 10.000 oranges to all apple/orange token holders. Distribution will be proportional to how many fruits the token holders have left in the 2 piles" 

And basically that is it. To ensure the DEX works and swaps are possible, there needs to be a liquidity pool. To incentive people to contribute tokens to the pool and ensure the mechanism works there are these "Liquidity pool fees" and "Token Farming".

@xch0ix 
sooo when you go to Binance or w/e they act as the intermediate for two trading parties. However on a DEX there is no central entity who facilitates the trade.

Instead you have an AMM (automated market maker) where people have to supply the two parts of a trade instead. 

The transaction fee binance takes is instead paid out to liquidity pool providers
So in an ideal world say you provide ADA/BTC for a liquidity position. While you have your LP put into the DEX you're earning in 2 ways:
1. transaction fees that basically provide you more tokens when you pull them out
2. the native DEX token in the form of an APR

The risks come into play where there's exploitable smart contracts (Rug risk #1), a sudden drop in liquidity in the pool (Rug risk #2), or the price ratio or your assets drastically changes from the point in time where you added to the liquidity pool (Impermanent loss). There's also other scam risks like squid game, call that rug risk 3.

The protocol basically rebalances periodically to maintain the same ratio of your pair so if you have BTC/ADA pair and ADA pumps 10% and BTC doesn't, the protocol essentially sells ADA for BTC so you maintain the same ratio on your position. That's referred to as impermanent loss which once you understand is not so scary. Like BTC will pump 5% and ADA will pump 10% so your position will increase in value only like 8% or something (edited)

When you add 1 WBNB and 100 COPI (since, in our example 1 WBNB = 100 COPI) as a liquidity pair, impermanent loss can occur if the two assets do not rise or fall in tandem.
